For Gaussian pure-loss dynamics -- the canonical model of continuous-variable decoherence in optical attenuation channels, squeezed-light interferometric sensing, and superconducting bosonic architectures -- complete positivity, the requirement that the dynamics remain physical even for systems entangled with an ancilla, creates an exact phase boundary at which the minimum reverse cost vanishes, fixes the reverse-noise budget on both sides, and makes pure nonclassical targets dynamically singular. The minimum reverse cost vanishes exactly at a critical squeezing-to-thermal ratio and is strictly positive away from it, with a sharp asymmetry: below the boundary, standard reverse prescriptions such as the fixed-diffusion Bayes reverse remain feasible at mild cost; above it, these prescriptions become infeasible, the covariance-aligned generator remains CP-feasible and uniquely optimal, and the cost can be severe. The optimal reverse noise is locked to the state's own fluctuation geometry and simultaneously minimizes the geometric, metrological, and thermodynamic price of reversal. For multimode trajectories, the exact cost is additive in a canonical set of mode-resolved data, and a globally continuous protocol attains this optimum on every mixed-state interval. If a pure nonclassical endpoint is included, the same pointwise law holds for every $t>0$, but the optimum diverges as $2/t$: exact reversal of a pure quantum state is dynamically unattainable. These results establish an exact law of quantum reversibility in the canonical pure-loss setting and provide a sharp benchmark for broader theories of quantum reverse diffusion.

AI.tldr: Quantum reverse diffusion for Gaussian pure-loss dynamics exhibits an exact phase boundary where minimum reverse cost vanishes at critical squeezing-to-thermal ratio, with sharp asymmetry between regimes and fundamental impossibility of exact pure-state reversal.
AI.motivation: To establish exact laws of quantum reversibility in the canonical pure-loss setting (Gaussian pure-loss dynamics) that models continuous-variable decoherence in optical attenuation, squeezed-light interferometric sensing, and superconducting bosonic architectures, and to understand how complete positivity requirements affect reverse diffusion feasibility and costs.
AI.method: Analysis of quantum reverse diffusion for Gaussian pure-loss dynamics, examining complete positivity constraints, deriving exact phase boundaries, determining optimal reverse-noise budgets, and analyzing different reverse prescriptions including fixed-diffusion Bayes reverse and covariance-aligned generator approaches.
AI.result: Found exact phase boundary at critical squeezing-to-thermal ratio where minimum reverse cost vanishes; sharp asymmetry: below boundary standard reverse prescriptions feasible at mild cost, above boundary standard prescriptions become infeasible while covariance-aligned generator remains CP-feasible and uniquely optimal; pure nonclassical targets are dynamically singular; optimal reverse noise locked to state's fluctuation geometry; multimode cost additive in canonical mode-resolved data; exact pure-state reversal dynamically unattainable with optimum diverging as 2/t.
AI.conclusion: Establishes exact law of quantum reversibility for Gaussian pure-loss dynamics, provides sharp benchmark for broader quantum reverse diffusion theories, reveals fundamental limitations on pure-state reversal, and demonstrates how complete positivity constraints create phase boundaries and dictate optimal reverse strategies.

title: Fair Decoder Baselines and Rigorous Finite-Size Scaling for Bivariate Bicycle Codes on the Quantum Erasure Channel
summary: Fair threshold estimation for bivariate bicycle (BB) codes on the quantum erasure channel runs into two recurring problems: decoder-baseline unfairness and the conflation of finite-size pseudo-thresholds with true asymptotic thresholds. We run both uninformed and \emph{erasure-aware} minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) surface code baselines alongside BP-OSD decoding of BB codes. With standard depolarizing-weight MWPM and no erasure information, performance matches random guessing on the erasure channel in our tested regime -- so prior work that compares against this baseline is really comparing decoders, not codes. Using 200{,}000 shots per point and bootstrap confidence intervals, we sweep five BB code sizes from $N=144$ to $N=1296$. Pseudo-thresholds (WER = 0.10) run from $p^* = 0.370$ to $0.471$; finite-size scaling (FSS) gives an asymptotic threshold $p^*_\infty \approx 0.488$, within 2.4\% of the zero-rate limit and without maximum-likelihood decoding. On the fair baseline, BB at $N=1296$ has a modest edge in threshold over the surface code at twice the qubit count, and a 12$\times$ lower normalized overhead -- the latter is where the practical advantage sits. All runs are reproducible from recorded seeds and package versions.

AI.tldr: BB codes show modest threshold advantage over surface codes on quantum erasure channel with 12× lower normalized overhead, achieving asymptotic threshold p*∞ ≈ 0.488 using BP-OSD decoding.
AI.motivation: Address two recurring problems in fair threshold estimation for bivariate bicycle (BB) codes: decoder-baseline unfairness and conflation of finite-size pseudo-thresholds with true asymptotic thresholds, particularly on the quantum erasure channel.
AI.method: Compare both uninformed and erasure-aware MWPM surface code baselines with BP-OSD decoding of BB codes. Use 200,000 shots per point with bootstrap confidence intervals, sweep five BB code sizes from N=144 to N=1296. Employ finite-size scaling for asymptotic threshold estimation.
AI.result: Pseudo-thresholds (WER = 0.10) range from p* = 0.370 to 0.471; finite-size scaling gives asymptotic threshold p*∞ ≈ 0.488, within 2.4% of zero-rate limit. BB at N=1296 shows modest threshold edge over surface code at twice qubit count with 12× lower normalized overhead.
AI.conclusion: BB codes demonstrate practical advantage over surface codes on quantum erasure channel primarily through significantly lower normalized overhead (12× reduction), with fair baseline comparisons showing previous work comparing decoders rather than codes when using uninformed MWPM baselines.

title: Photon-echo synchronization and quantum state transfer in short quantum links
summary: The short quantum link regime, where the photon travel time $τ$ is comparable to the emitter lifetime $1/γ$, is experimentally relevant but theoretically underexplored: existing few-mode descriptions lose validity as retardation and multimode effects become significant. Using a Delay Differential Equation (DDE) framework that admits exact analytical solutions from the single-mode cavity limit to the multimode waveguide continuum, we show that emitters coupled to a short link spontaneously lock into self-synchronized Rabi oscillations driven by coherent photon echoes, breaking the link's discrete time-displacement symmetry. The resulting spectral structure -- persistent quasi-dark states and vacuum Rabi splitting, including in the superstrong coupling regime -- enables efficient quantum state transfer (QST): benchmarking three protocols across the full $γτ$ parameter space, we find that STIRAP exploits the quasi-dark-state structure to achieve a quadratic infidelity floor $\mathcal{O}((γτ)^2)$, outperforming both SWAP (linear error $\mathcal{O}(γτ)$) and wavepacket engineering for $γτ\lesssim 1.44$, even in regimes where retardation cannot be neglected. These results establish photon-echo synchronization as an engineering resource for quantum state transfer, with DDE modeling providing the exact analytical predictions needed to design and optimize short-link experiments on current circuit-QED hardware.

AI.tldr: Short quantum links (photon travel time comparable to emitter lifetime) enable self-synchronized Rabi oscillations via photon echoes, breaking time-displacement symmetry and creating quasi-dark states that enhance quantum state transfer, with STIRAP outperforming other protocols in this regime.
AI.motivation: The short quantum link regime (τ ~ 1/γ) is experimentally relevant but theoretically underexplored because existing few-mode descriptions fail when retardation and multimode effects become significant. Current circuit-QED hardware operates in this regime, requiring new theoretical frameworks.
AI.method: Developed a Delay Differential Equation (DDE) framework that provides exact analytical solutions spanning from single-mode cavity limit to multimode waveguide continuum. Used this framework to analyze emitter dynamics and benchmark three quantum state transfer protocols (STIRAP, SWAP, wavepacket engineering) across the full γτ parameter space.
AI.result: Emitters coupled to short links spontaneously lock into self-synchronized Rabi oscillations driven by coherent photon echoes, breaking the link's discrete time-displacement symmetry. This creates persistent quasi-dark states and vacuum Rabi splitting, even in superstrong coupling. STIRAP exploits quasi-dark-state structure to achieve quadratic infidelity floor O((γτ)²), outperforming SWAP (linear error O(γτ)) and wavepacket engineering for γτ ≲ 1.44.
AI.conclusion: Photon-echo synchronization serves as an engineering resource for quantum state transfer, with the DDE framework providing exact analytical predictions needed to design and optimize short-link experiments on current circuit-QED hardware. STIRAP is optimal for practical short-link regimes.

title: Utility-scale quantum computational chemistry
summary: Chemistry and materials science are widely regarded as potential killer application fields for quantum hardware. While the dream of unlocking unprecedented simulation capabilities remains compelling, quantum algorithm development must adapt to the evolving constraints of the emerging quantum hardware in order to accomplish any advantage for the computational chemistry practice. At the same time, the continuous advancement of classical wavefunction-theory methods narrows the window for a broad quantum advantage. Here, we explore potential benefits of quantum computation from the broader perspective of utility-scale applications. We argue that quantum algorithms need not only enable accurate calculations for a few challenging, that is strongly correlated, molecular structures, that might be hard to describe with traditional methods. Instead, they must also support the practical integration of quantum-accelerated computations into high-throughput pipelines for routine calculations on arbitrary molecules, ultimately delivering a tangible value to society.

AI.tldr: Quantum computing for chemistry must adapt to hardware constraints and focus on practical integration into high-throughput pipelines rather than just solving strongly correlated problems.
AI.motivation: While quantum computing holds promise for chemistry and materials science, quantum algorithms must evolve to match emerging hardware constraints and compete with advancing classical methods to achieve practical advantage.
AI.method: The paper explores quantum computing benefits from a utility-scale perspective, arguing for integration of quantum-accelerated computations into routine high-throughput pipelines rather than focusing solely on strongly correlated systems.
AI.result: The analysis suggests quantum algorithms must support practical integration into computational workflows for arbitrary molecules to deliver tangible societal value, not just enable accurate calculations for challenging molecular structures.
AI.conclusion: Quantum advantage in chemistry requires algorithms that work within hardware constraints and integrate into practical high-throughput pipelines for routine calculations, moving beyond just solving strongly correlated problems to deliver broader societal value.

title: Practical Quantum Broadcasting
comment: 6 pages (main text) + 58 pages (supplemental material), packed with extensive figures and illustrations. Comments welcome!
summary: Incorporating sample efficiency, by requiring the number of states consumed by broadcasting does not exceed that of a naive prepare-and-distribute strategy, gives rise to the no practical quantum broadcasting theorem. To navigate this limitation, we introduce approximate and probabilistic virtual broadcasting and derive analytic expressions for their optimal sample complexity overheads. Allowing deviations at the receivers restores sample efficiency even in the 1-to-2 approximate setting, whereas probabilistic protocols obey a stronger no-go theorem that excludes all sample efficient 1-to-2 implementations for arbitrary dimension and success probability. Rather counterintuitive, this obstruction does not persist at larger receiver numbers: for qubit systems, practical 1-to-6 virtual broadcasting becomes attainable. These results elevate sample complexity from a technical constraint to a defining operational principle, opening an unexplored route to the efficient distribution of quantum information.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a "no practical quantum broadcasting theorem" based on sample efficiency constraints, introduces approximate and probabilistic virtual broadcasting protocols, and shows that while 1-to-2 probabilistic broadcasting remains impossible, practical 1-to-6 broadcasting becomes achievable for qubit systems.
AI.motivation: To overcome the fundamental limitations of quantum broadcasting (the no-cloning theorem) by introducing sample efficiency as a practical constraint, enabling the development of protocols that can efficiently distribute quantum information despite theoretical impossibility of perfect broadcasting.
AI.method: Introduces two approaches: (1) approximate virtual broadcasting that allows deviations at receivers, and (2) probabilistic virtual broadcasting. Derives analytic expressions for optimal sample complexity overheads and analyzes protocols under sample efficiency constraints where the number of states consumed cannot exceed that of naive prepare-and-distribute strategies.
AI.result: Approximate broadcasting restores sample efficiency even in 1-to-2 settings when allowing receiver deviations. Probabilistic protocols obey a stronger no-go theorem excluding all sample efficient 1-to-2 implementations for arbitrary dimension and success probability. Counterintuitively, practical 1-to-6 virtual broadcasting becomes attainable for qubit systems, showing the obstruction doesn't persist at larger receiver numbers.
AI.conclusion: Sample complexity should be elevated from a technical constraint to a defining operational principle for quantum information distribution. The work opens an unexplored route to efficient quantum information distribution by showing that practical broadcasting becomes possible when moving beyond 1-to-2 scenarios, particularly for qubit systems with 1-to-6 broadcasting.

title: Active Quantum Particles from Engineered Dissipation
summary: We introduce and characterize different models for an active quantum particle where activity arises from engineered dissipation-- specifically, from a suitably coupled nonequilibrium environment. These include a model of a particle moving on a lattice with coherent and dissipative hopping, as well as quantum generalizations of well-studied models of active behavior, such as the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, run-and-tumble dynamics, and the active Brownian particle. Despite the different microscopic mechanisms at play, we show that all these models display key features of active motion. Notably, we observe a crossover from diffusive to active-diffusive behavior at long times, leading to an effective Péclet number, as well as a strong sensitivity to boundary conditions which, in our open quantum system context, arises from the Liouville skin effect. We discuss the role of quantum fluctuations and experimental realizations with superconducting circuits or cold gases, closing with perspectives for many-body effects in quantum active matter.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quantum models of active particles where activity emerges from engineered dissipation, showing they exhibit key features of active motion including diffusive-to-active-diffusive crossover and boundary sensitivity from the Liouville skin effect.
AI.motivation: To develop quantum models of active particles where activity arises from engineered dissipation rather than biological processes, bridging active matter physics with quantum open systems and exploring quantum effects in active motion.
AI.method: Introduces several quantum models including: (1) particle on lattice with coherent and dissipative hopping, (2) quantum generalizations of classical active models (active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, run-and-tumble, active Brownian particle). Uses open quantum system formalism with engineered dissipation to create activity.
AI.result: All models display key active motion features: crossover from diffusive to active-diffusive behavior at long times with effective Péclet number, strong sensitivity to boundary conditions due to Liouville skin effect in open quantum systems. Demonstrates quantum fluctuations play a role.
AI.conclusion: Engineered dissipation can create quantum active particles with properties analogous to classical active matter, opening possibilities for experimental realization with superconducting circuits or cold gases, and future exploration of many-body quantum active matter effects.

title: Entanglement assisted communication complexity measured by distinguishability
summary: We investigate the quantum advantage that can arise in typical two-party communication scenarios, where the sender and the receiver are allowed to share prior correlations. Focusing on communication tasks constrained by the distinguishability of the sender's inputs, we demonstrate that entanglement-assisted communication, both classical and quantum, can outperform classical communication supplemented with shared randomness. We begin by developing a general framework for communication tasks with pre-shared correlations. We identify certain communication tasks that exhibit an advantage under entanglement assistance compared to classical communication. Through these results, we establish a connection between quantum communication and entanglement-assisted classical communication, and also show an equivalence between entanglement-assisted classical communication and entanglement-assisted quantum communication. We then consider the simplest scenarios in which the receiver has no input and demonstrate that entanglement-assisted strategies still offer advantages over both classical communication and quantum communication without prior entanglement. Finally, by constructing a class of communication tasks, we show that a non-maximally entangled state can, in some cases, be more useful than a maximally entangled state as a pre-shared resource.

AI.tldr: Quantum communication with entanglement assistance outperforms classical communication with shared randomness in certain two-party tasks, with non-maximally entangled states sometimes being more useful than maximally entangled ones.
AI.motivation: To investigate quantum advantages in two-party communication scenarios where sender and receiver share prior correlations, focusing on tasks constrained by input distinguishability and comparing entanglement-assisted strategies with classical communication supplemented by shared randomness.
AI.method: Developed a general framework for communication tasks with pre-shared correlations, identified specific tasks showing entanglement advantage, established connections between different communication models, examined simplest scenarios (receiver has no input), and constructed a class of communication tasks to compare different entangled states.
AI.result: Entanglement-assisted communication (both classical and quantum) outperforms classical communication with shared randomness; entanglement-assisted strategies offer advantages over both classical communication and quantum communication without prior entanglement; non-maximally entangled states can be more useful than maximally entangled states as pre-shared resources in some cases.
AI.conclusion: Quantum correlations provide genuine advantages in communication tasks beyond classical shared randomness, with entanglement serving as a valuable resource that can enhance communication performance, sometimes even more effectively when the entanglement is not maximized.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography from Quantum Stabilizer Decoding
summary: Post-quantum cryptography currently rests on a small number of hardness assumptions, posing significant risks should any one of them be compromised. This vulnerability motivates the search for new and cryptographically versatile assumptions that make a convincing case for quantum hardness. In this work, we argue that decoding random quantum stabilizer codes -- a quantum analog of the well-studied LPN problem -- is an excellent candidate. This task occupies a unique middle ground: it is inherently native to quantum computation, yet admits an equivalent formulation with purely classical input and output, as recently shown by Khesin et al. (STOC '26). We prove that the average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding implies the core primitives of classical Cryptomania, including public-key encryption (PKE) and oblivious transfer (OT), as well as one-way functions. Our constructions are moreover practical: our PKE scheme achieves essentially the same efficiency as state-of-the-art LPN-based PKE, and our OT is round-optimal. We also provide substantial evidence that stabilizer decoding does not reduce to LPN, suggesting that the former problem constitutes a genuinely new post-quantum assumption. Our primary technical contributions are twofold. First, we give a reduction from random quantum stabilizer decoding to an average-case problem closely resembling LPN, but which is equipped with additional symplectic algebraic structure. While this structure is essential to the quantum nature of the problem, it raises significant barriers to cryptographic security reductions. Second, we develop a new suit of scrambling techniques for such structured linear spaces, and use them to produce rigorous security proofs for all of our constructions.

AI.tldr: Quantum stabilizer code decoding proposed as new post-quantum hardness assumption enabling practical PKE and OT with efficiency comparable to LPN-based schemes.
AI.motivation: Current post-quantum cryptography relies on few hardness assumptions, creating significant risk if any are broken. Need new quantum-hard assumptions with cryptographic versatility.
AI.method: Propose decoding random quantum stabilizer codes as quantum analog of LPN. Reduce to average-case problem with symplectic algebraic structure. Develop scrambling techniques for structured linear spaces to enable security proofs.
AI.result: Show average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding implies classical Cryptomania primitives (PKE, OT, one-way functions). Construct practical PKE with efficiency matching state-of-the-art LPN-based PKE and round-optimal OT. Provide evidence stabilizer decoding doesn't reduce to LPN.
AI.conclusion: Quantum stabilizer decoding is promising new post-quantum hardness assumption with cryptographic versatility, practical efficiency, and evidence of being distinct from existing assumptions like LPN.

title: Low-weight quantum syndrome errors in belief propagation decoding
summary: We describe an empirical approach to identify low-weight combinations of columns of the decoding matrices of a quantum circuit-level noise model, for which belief-propagation (BP) algorithms converge possibly very slowly. Focusing on the logical-idle syndrome cycle of the low-density parity check gross code, we identify criteria providing a characterization of the Tanner subgraph of such low-weight error syndromes. We analyze the dynamics of iterations when BP is used to decode weight-four and weight-five errors, finding statistics akin to exponential activation in the presence of noise or escape from chaotic phase-space domains. We study how BP convergence improves when adding to the decoding matrix relevant combinations of fault columns, and show that the suggested decoder amendment can result in the reduction of both logical errors and decoding time.

AI.tldr: Empirical approach identifies low-weight error syndromes where BP decoding converges slowly in quantum circuits; decoder amendment improves convergence and reduces logical errors.
AI.motivation: To address slow convergence of belief-propagation algorithms in quantum error correction, particularly for low-weight error syndromes in circuit-level noise models.
AI.method: Empirical identification of low-weight column combinations in decoding matrices; analysis of BP dynamics for weight-4/5 errors; characterization of Tanner subgraphs; decoder amendment by adding relevant fault columns.
AI.result: Identified criteria for problematic Tanner subgraphs; observed exponential activation/chaotic escape dynamics; demonstrated improved BP convergence and reduced logical errors with decoder amendments.
AI.conclusion: Targeted decoder amendments addressing specific low-weight error syndromes can significantly improve BP convergence and reduce logical error rates in quantum error correction.

title: Quantum block encoding for semiseparable matrices
summary:
Quantum block encoding (QBE) is a crucial step in the development of most quantum algorithms, as it provides an embedding of a given matrix into a suitable larger unitary matrix. Historically, the development of efficient techniques for QBE has mostly focused on sparse matrices; less effort has been devoted to data-sparse (e.g., rank-structured) matrices.
  In this work we examine a particular case of rank structure, namely, one-pair semiseparable matrices. We present a new block encoding approach that relies on a suitable factorization of the given matrix as the product of triangular and diagonal factors. To encode the matrix, the algorithm needs $2\log(N)+7$ ancillary qubits. This process takes polylogarithmic time and has an error of $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$, where $N$ is the matrix size.

AI.tldr: A quantum block encoding method for one-pair semiseparable matrices using triangular-diagonal factorization with 2log(N)+7 ancilla qubits, polylogarithmic time, and O(N²) error.
AI.motivation: Quantum block encoding has focused primarily on sparse matrices, leaving data-sparse/rank-structured matrices like semiseparable matrices underdeveloped despite their practical importance.
AI.method: Factorizes one-pair semiseparable matrices into triangular and diagonal factors, then encodes these factors into quantum circuits using 2log(N)+7 ancillary qubits with polylogarithmic time complexity.
AI.result: Achieves efficient quantum block encoding for one-pair semiseparable matrices with ancilla qubit scaling of 2log(N)+7, polylogarithmic time, and error scaling of O(N²).
AI.conclusion: The method extends quantum block encoding capabilities to rank-structured matrices, specifically one-pair semiseparable matrices, providing an efficient encoding scheme with favorable qubit and time complexity.

title: Quantum Structures as Generative Scores: Partition Logic, Generative Logic, and Aesthetic Form
summary: We connect partition logic with Generative Logic by translating finite partition logics into Prolog-based Simple Generative Logic Grammars. As a proof of concept, we use the five-atom V-logic L_{12} to generate a modular visual artifact, the \emph{Quantum Square}. The approach separates logical structure from its visual, textual, or sonic realization. This makes partition logic useful both as a generative design resource and as a tool for communicating complementarity.

AI.tldr: Translation of partition logic into Prolog-based generative grammars enables creation of modular visual artifacts like Quantum Square, separating logical structure from realization.
AI.motivation: To bridge partition logic with generative logic, making partition logic useful as both a generative design resource and a tool for communicating complementarity concepts.
AI.method: Translate finite partition logics into Prolog-based Simple Generative Logic Grammars, demonstrated using the five-atom V-logic L_{12} to generate the Quantum Square artifact.
AI.result: Successfully connected partition logic with generative logic, creating a modular visual artifact (Quantum Square) while separating logical structure from visual/textual/sonic realization.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables partition logic to serve dual purposes: as a generative design framework and as a communication tool for complementarity, with potential applications in design and conceptual visualization.

title: Measurement-Induced Quantum Neural Network
summary: We introduce a measurement-induced quantum neural network (MINN), an adaptive monitored-circuit architecture in which mid-circuit measurement outcomes determine the entangling gates in subsequent layers. In contrast to standard monitored circuits where sites and gates are sampled randomly, the gates are parametrized and variational, producing correlated history-dependent dynamics and injecting nonlinearity through measurement back-action. A generic MINN is not expected to be efficiently classically simulable. To demonstrate feasibility, we study a matchgate MINN that admits exact fermionic simulation and can be trained with gradient estimators. We apply the architecture to continuous optimization, image classification, and ground-state search in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, finding effective training and performance over a broad range of monitoring rates.

AI.tldr: A measurement-induced quantum neural network (MINN) uses mid-circuit measurement outcomes to adaptively control subsequent entangling gates, creating history-dependent dynamics with measurement back-action nonlinearity, and is demonstrated through a matchgate variant for various computational tasks.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum neural network architecture that leverages measurement-induced dynamics for enhanced computational capabilities beyond standard monitored circuits, addressing the need for adaptive, nonlinear quantum processing with classical intractability guarantees.
AI.method: Introduces a measurement-induced quantum neural network (MINN) where mid-circuit measurement outcomes determine subsequent entangling gates in an adaptive manner. Uses parametrized variational gates that create correlated history-dependent dynamics. Studies a matchgate MINN variant that admits exact fermionic simulation and can be trained with gradient estimators.
AI.result: Demonstrates feasibility through applications to continuous optimization, image classification, and ground-state search in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass. Shows effective training and performance across a broad range of monitoring rates. The matchgate MINN variant provides exact simulation capabilities while maintaining the adaptive architecture.
AI.conclusion: MINN represents a novel quantum neural network architecture that harnesses measurement back-action for nonlinear processing, offers classical intractability for generic cases, and demonstrates practical feasibility through specialized variants applicable to diverse computational tasks.

title: Quantum theory based on real numbers cannot be experimentally falsified
comment: 60 pages (7 main, 10 technical material, 43 appendices), 5 figures (4 in main, 1 in appendix)
summary: Whether the complex numbers of standard quantum theory are experimentally indispensable has remained open for decades. Real quantum theory (RQT), obtained by replacing complex amplitudes with real ones while retaining the usual Kronecker-product composition rule, reproduces all single-party and bipartite Bell correlations of quantum theory (QT), but its lack of local tomography suggested that the two theories might diverge in more general local experiments. This possibility appeared to be confirmed by Renou et al., who argued that a bilocal network experiment can falsify RQT without falsifying QT. Here we show that this conclusion relies on an experimentally untestable assumption. The key distinction is between product-state independence, which constrains the mathematical form of source states, and operational independence, which is defined entirely by the absence of observable cross-source correlations. We prove that, once source independence is imposed operationally, every finite network correlation achievable in QT is also achievable in RQT with the same locality structure of the measurements. We then extend this equivalence to arbitrary finite sequential multipartite protocols involving channels and measurements with prescribed locality structure. Thus, as long as no violation of QT is observed, RQT cannot be experimentally falsified. Our results restore the empirical indistinguishability of QT and RQT, while showing that they support markedly different pictures of the correlation structure underlying the same observed world.

AI.tldr: Real quantum theory (RQT) is empirically indistinguishable from standard quantum theory (QT) when source independence is imposed operationally rather than as product-state independence, contrary to previous claims that network experiments could falsify RQT.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing question of whether complex numbers in quantum theory are experimentally indispensable by examining whether real quantum theory (RQT) can be distinguished from standard quantum theory (QT) in network experiments, particularly addressing previous claims that RQT could be falsified in bilocal network experiments.
AI.method: Distinguishes between product-state independence (mathematical form constraint) and operational independence (absence of observable cross-source correlations), then proves that with operational independence, all finite network correlations achievable in QT are also achievable in RQT with the same measurement locality structure, extending this to arbitrary finite sequential multipartite protocols with channels and measurements.
AI.result: RQT cannot be experimentally falsified as long as no violation of QT is observed, restoring empirical indistinguishability between QT and RQT while showing they support different pictures of correlation structure underlying the same observed world.
AI.conclusion: Complex numbers in standard quantum theory are not experimentally indispensable for reproducing observed correlations, as RQT with operational source independence can reproduce all finite network correlations of QT, making the two theories empirically indistinguishable despite their different mathematical structures.

title: The commutant of fermionic Gaussian unitaries
summary: In this work, we characterize the $t$-th order commutants of fermionic Gaussian unitaries and of their particle-preserving subgroup acting on $n$ fermionic modes. These commutants govern Haar averages over the corresponding groups and therefore play a central role in fermionic randomized protocols, invariant theory, and resource quantification. Using Howe dualities, we show that the particle-preserving commutant is generated by generalized copy-hopping operators, while that for general Gaussian commutant is generated by generalized quadratic Majorana bilinears together with parity. We then derive closed formulas for the dimensions of both commutants as functions of $t$ and $n$, and develop constructive Gelfand--Tsetlin procedures to obtain explicit orthonormal bases, with detailed low-$t$ examples. Our framework also clarifies the structure of replicated fermionic states and connects naturally to measures of fermionic correlations, generalized Plücker-type constraints, and the stabilizer entropy of fermionic Gaussian states. These results provide a unified algebraic description of higher-order invariants for fermionic Gaussian dynamics.

AI.tldr: Characterizes t-th order commutants of fermionic Gaussian unitaries and their particle-preserving subgroup, providing algebraic foundations for fermionic randomized protocols and invariant theory.
AI.motivation: Commutants govern Haar averages over fermionic groups, playing central roles in fermionic randomized protocols, invariant theory, and resource quantification, requiring systematic characterization.
AI.method: Uses Howe dualities to show particle-preserving commutant generated by generalized copy-hopping operators, general Gaussian commutant by generalized quadratic Majorana bilinears with parity; derives dimension formulas and develops constructive Gelfand-Tsetlin procedures for orthonormal bases.
AI.result: Obtains closed formulas for commutant dimensions as functions of t and n, constructs explicit orthonormal bases with low-t examples, clarifies structure of replicated fermionic states, connects to fermionic correlation measures and generalized Plücker constraints.
AI.conclusion: Provides unified algebraic description of higher-order invariants for fermionic Gaussian dynamics, establishing foundations for fermionic randomized protocols, invariant theory, and resource quantification.
